notes.1a: Generally good marks here. The commonest mistakes were to classify manufacturing wages as a factory overhead and to include Sales in the manufacturing account.
notes.1b: Again, good marks in general. Errors included miscalculation of the reduction in the provision for doubtful debts and classifying income from rent as an expense.
notes.1c: Well presented by most candidates. Common errors were recording only one of the closing stocks, entering the wrong adjustments for the debtors figure and classifying the bank overdraft as a current asset.
notes.2: This question was very poorly attempted by most candidates, though a few did attain full marks.
notes.2a: (i) This would have been best attempted using Disposal accounts, but only around half of the candidates tried to use these, and of these only a very small number - around two to three percent - gained full marks. Calculations were equally acceptable, but again very few did well here. Commonly, the machinery disposal was calculated, then one of the disposals of motor vehicles was calculated but the second disposal of motor vehicles was often ignored.
notes.2aii: The fixed asset schedule was very much a discriminator. Few, if any, of the candidates were used to this presentation but the more able worked out the rates of depreciation from the given schedule and could apply them in their answer.
notes.2b: (i) The question asked for the causes of depreciation – this was interpreted by a large minority as the methods of depreciation, and answering on that basis gained no marks. Those who correctly understood the question usually gained at least two marks, for Wear and Tear and Obsolescence, and some gained a third mark for Time or Depletion.
notes.2bii: Those who answered (b)(i) correctly usually did well enough in (b)(ii).
notes.2c: Some good answers here, though some candidates discussed the various methods of depreciation which did not gain marks.
notes.3a: The vast majority of candidates understood these concepts and were able to communicate their understanding.
notes.3b: As the question gave the formula, most candidates gained full marks here, though some did not seem to understand the word Percentage (%) and gave the answer as 3.5:1 or 7/20.
notes.3c: Many correct answers here but almost half tried to use the formula of Fixed Costs divided by Unit Contribution, and as Unit Contribution was not available those candidates usually gained only one mark.
notes.3d: and (e) Usually some marks scored here, though fewer gained full marks.
notes.3f: This was a good discriminator with many candidates giving the answer $469 000, as they saw a reduction in sales price as being synonymous with a reduction in sales quantity.
